concept_name: The Unit Circle Unrolled into Sine and Cosine
section: 3.1 — Trigonometric Functions (the unit circle, radian measure, sine and cosine graphs)
source_book: NCERT Mathematics Class 11, Chapter 3 'Trigonometric Functions' — chapter-index scope reference only; teaching, examples and phrasing authored from first principles. NCERT Exemplar consulted for misconception beliefs only. IB DP AA, AP Precalculus, Cambridge 0606/0580 and A-level Pure specifications consulted for COVERAGE SCOPE only (curriculum_tags). HC Verma and DC Pandey are physics-only sources and were not consulted. First mathematics concept through the pipeline.

real_world_anchor.primary: The tip of a clock's second hand. A classroom wall clock anywhere in the world carries a genuinely rotating radius of fixed length — the exact apparatus of this sim. It turns an object a student has stared at their whole life into the answer to 'where does the wavy graph actually come from'. Delivered verbatim in STATE_1's narration, inside its word budget.

theta.name: angle of the point from the positive horizontal axis, DEGREES, anticlockwise

phi.name: sweep parameter for the bright drawn curve, DEGREES — choreography-only, NEVER a slider (the phi law, F1)

phi_r.name: sweep parameter for the dim recap curve, DEGREES — choreography-only, NEVER a slider (the phi law, F1)

constraints: domain: sin θ and cos θ are defined for EVERY real θ, no excluded points, no asymptotes (this concept deliberately never introduces tan θ, which would add excluded points at θ = π/2 + kπ)

r ≡ 1 in every state, always — no primitive in this concept draws a circle or arc at a live radius (body.size and angle_arc.radius are both number-only in this renderer; the amplitude state was cut for exactly this reason)

the two scale factors are declared ONCE and reused verbatim in every expression: S_v = 110 px/unit (circle radius AND both wave ordinates), S_h = 46 px/rad (wave horizontal axis) — applied to the RADIAN conversion of theta/phi (e.g. 46*phi*PI/180), never to the raw degree number; circle centre (150,230), wave origin x0=300, baseline y=230
phi and phi_r are choreography-only in every state — NEVER authored as a slider variable (the phi law, F1); every locus_trace x_expr/y_expr references ONLY phi or phi_r, never theta

wherever a pen or carrier is on screen, theta and that trace's own sweep parameter are numerically EQUAL at every instant (the equality invariant, F18) — enforced by giving theta and phi the SAME from/to/start_ms/duration_ms in every state where both are choreographed together

theta, phi and phi_r are DEGREES everywhere — native to the slider caption and to drawAngleArc; every trig-consuming expression converts inline via *PI/180; the derived key s is the honest radian value (and, since r≡1, simultaneously the taught arc length) — never confuse the engine variable theta (degrees) with the mathematical symbol θ in a formula surface (radians, i.e. s)

STATE_1.title: A Point Moves Round a Circle

tts_sentences.text_en: A point travels round a circle of radius one, starting at the rightmost point and turning anticlockwise.
This circle is like the tip of a clock's second hand, turning steadily round a fixed centre.
The angle theta measures how far it has turned.
As the point turns, it sweeps out a distance along the rim.
Because the radius is one, that rim distance and the angle are the same number.
That number is the angle in radians, and a full turn is two pi.
Watch the counter: the arc length s and the angle theta stay equal.

STATE_3.title: Sine Is the Height of the Point

misconception_watch.belief: sine belongs to right triangles: it is undefined past 90° and never negative
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the height segment continues through 90° and 180°; below the horizontal line it hangs downward and the readout shows −0.50 at θ = 210°
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: sin θ is the point's signed height — any angle, any sign.

tts_sentences.text_en: Sine of theta is the height of the point above the horizontal line.
For angles up to ninety degrees this is the same sine you know from right triangles; the circle just keeps going where the triangle stops.
Past one hundred and eighty degrees the point sits below the line, so the height reads negative.

STATE_4.title: Height Carried Sideways Makes the Wave

misconception_watch.belief: the wave is a picture of the path the point travels
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the closed circle and the wave stay two distinct objects in two zones; the dashed carrier shows the wave's horizontal position is the ANGLE, not a place the point visits
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: the wave plots height against angle — the path stays a circle.

tts_sentences.text_en: Now carry that height sideways as the angle grows.
The horizontal axis is the angle, and the height at each angle is plotted above it.
The curve that draws itself is the sine wave.
The point still travels in a circle; the wave plots its height against the angle.

misconception_watch.belief: cos 0 = 0, by false analogy with sin 0 = 0 — both waves must start at zero
misconception_watch.visual_counter: the state opens at θ = 0 with the horizontal segment at full length under cos θ = 1.00 while the height segment is visibly zero — the believed value and the true value in one frame
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: at θ = 0 the point is farthest right, so cos 0 = 1.

tts_sentences.text_en: At the start the point is farthest right, so the horizontal distance is one, not zero.
That horizontal distance is cosine of theta.
Carry it sideways the same way and a second wave draws itself.
It is the same shape as the sine wave, a quarter turn ahead.
One full turn is finished, and the point starts round again.
The angle keeps counting past two pi, and the curve keeps going to the right.
The same heights come back in the same order, so the wave repeats.
Take one angle, then take the angle you get by reflecting it across the vertical line.
Both points sit at exactly the same height above the horizontal line.
So sine of pi minus theta equals sine of theta, at every angle you choose.
Drag the angle slider.
The point on the circle and the dots on both curves move together.

aha_moment.statement: The sine wave is the circling point's height, laid out along the angle.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: the dashed carrier holds point and pen at equal height while the curve unrolls

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered this concept when they can state the sign of sin θ in any quadrant, read an arc length off a radius-1 circle as the angle in radians, give cos 0 without reasoning from sin 0, say what each axis of the sine graph measures, name the period, and justify sin(π − θ) = sin θ from the picture rather than from a memorised table.

questions.stem: A point moves round the unit circle. What is the sign of sin θ at θ = 210°?

options.D: sin θ is not defined past 180°

distractor_misconceptions.B: reads the height as a plain length, so it can never be negative
distractor_misconceptions.C: confuses 210° with 180°, the angle where the height really is zero
distractor_misconceptions.D: M1 — believes sine belongs to right triangles and stops existing past 90°

questions.tested_idea: sin θ is the SIGNED height of the point, negative below the horizontal line
questions.parallel_form_stem: A point moves round the unit circle. What is the sign of sin θ at θ = 300°?

questions.stem: A point moves along a circle of radius 1 from θ = 0 to θ = π. What distance does it travel along the rim?

distractor_misconceptions.B: reads the angle in degrees and calls that number a length
distractor_misconceptions.C: gives the whole circumference instead of the half turn
distractor_misconceptions.D: uses the radius in place of the arc length

questions.tested_idea: on a radius-1 circle the arc length travelled equals the angle in radians
questions.parallel_form_stem: A point moves along a circle of radius 1 from θ = 0 to θ = π/2. What distance does it travel along the rim?

questions.stem: On the unit circle, what is the value of cos θ at θ = 0?

distractor_misconceptions.B: M3 — expects cosine to start at zero because sine does
distractor_misconceptions.C: reads the leftmost point of the circle instead of the rightmost
distractor_misconceptions.D: treats θ = 0 as a special case with no horizontal distance to measure

questions.tested_idea: cos θ is the signed horizontal distance, which is largest at θ = 0
questions.parallel_form_stem: On the unit circle, what is the value of sin θ at θ = π/2?

questions.stem: For any angle θ, what is sin(π − θ) in terms of sin θ?

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes reflecting the angle must flip the sign of the height
distractor_misconceptions.C: swaps the two coordinates of the reflected point
distractor_misconceptions.D: subtracts inside the function as if sine were linear

questions.tested_idea: mirror points about the vertical axis share one height, so sin(π−θ) = sin θ
questions.parallel_form_stem: For any angle θ, what is cos(−θ) in terms of cos θ?

questions.stem: On the graph built by carrying the point's height sideways, what does the horizontal axis measure?

options.B: The horizontal distance of the point from the centre
options.C: The time the point has been moving
options.D: The distance of the point from the graph

distractor_misconceptions.B: M2 — reads the wave as a picture of where the point actually goes
distractor_misconceptions.C: assumes the axis must be time because something is moving
distractor_misconceptions.D: treats the wave as a map of positions rather than a plot of height against angle

questions.tested_idea: the wave plots height against ANGLE; the path itself stays a circle
questions.parallel_form_stem: On the graph built by carrying the point's height sideways, what does the vertical axis measure?

questions.stem: The curve y = sin θ is continued to the right past θ = 2π. After what increase in θ do its values repeat?

distractor_misconceptions.B: a half turn puts the point on the opposite side of the circle, not back where it started
distractor_misconceptions.C: uses the quarter turn that separates the sine and cosine waves
distractor_misconceptions.D: assumes each new turn round the circle produces new heights

questions.tested_idea: one full turn returns the point to the same place, so the heights repeat every 2π
questions.parallel_form_stem: The curve y = cos θ is continued to the right past θ = 2π. After what increase in θ do its values repeat?
